description: We’re a multidisciplinary team passionate about engineering, data, software, AI, and space technology. For “Field Shift,” we aim to use NASA data to help farms adapt to changing environmental conditions. We’re looking for teammates skilled in GIS/remote sensing, agriculture, climate science, data analysis, AI/ML, web development, UI/UX, or storytelling. Curious, motivated learners are welcome!
summary: Field Shift is a decision-support tool that helps farmers compare crop rotations against NASA-derived weather, water and soil records. A farmer picks a region, sets priorities such as saving water or building soil, and sees their current rotation scored against three alternatives on water resilience, heat and frost safety, erosion protection, soil building, pest and disease break, and income. A field calendar shows when fields are bare during heavy rain or exposed to heat, frost or water stress. Scenario sliders warm or dry the climate, and each rotation is re-scored in 40 simulated futures, so the tool shows a range instead of one confident number. Every rotation lists its evidence, risks, data gaps and a checklist for a local expert, so the tool supports farmer judgment and does not replace it. A NASA POWER data pipeline is included to replace the demo climate values with real data.
details:
What it does. Field Shift lets a farmer choose a region, set priorities (water, soil, erosion, income, pests) and limits (irrigation water, livestock, whether residue stays on the field), then compares the current rotation with three alternatives. Each rotation is scored on six measures using a transparent monthly model: a soil water balance, crop heat and frost tolerance, ground cover during heavy-rain months, residue, nitrogen fixing and root depth, crop-family variety, and relative market value after weather risk. A field calendar shows bare-soil periods and stress months next to the monthly NASA-derived record (rain, maximum temperature, water demand, soil moisture, frost, heavy rain). A demo field map shows relative erosion, water stress and frost zones.

How it handles uncertainty. Each rotation is scored again in 40 simulated futures that vary temperature, rainfall, month-to-month weather and soil water capacity. The tool shows a score range and how often each alternative beats the current rotation, so farmers see how sure the result is.

Benefits and impact. It helps farmers explore rotations that protect soil, save water and adapt to a changing climate before committing a season. In the demo, swapping flooded rice for guar and mustard in Punjab cuts irrigation by about 80%, and adding cereal rye in Nebraska cuts bare-soil months from 16 of 24 to 2 of 24. It also says when a change will not help, for example a cover crop that does not break a maize disease cycle in Kenya.

NASA data. The model is built around a shared monthly record per location from NASA POWER (temperature, frost, rainfall, crop water demand), GPM IMERG (rainfall and heavy storms), SMAP (soil moisture), ECOSTRESS and MODIS (evapotranspiration), Landsat and MODIS NDVI (bare-field periods), GRACE-FO (groundwater trend) and SRTM (slope). The prototype includes a pipeline script that builds the monthly record from NASA POWER. Other sources are used as design references or marked as planned.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file with no server; a pure JavaScript scoring engine tested in Node; a Python script (standard library only) for NASA POWER; PptxGenJS for the slides.

What makes it creative. It turns satellite-style data into questions a farmer asks ("when is my soil bare during heavy rain?"), uses a transparent rule set that can be explained, and reports honest ranges and gaps instead of a single answer.

Factors we considered. Farmer priorities and constraints, local review by agronomists, the difference between satellite and ground data, and limits we state openly: the demo climate values are illustrative, crop and market values are simplified, the field map uses synthetic terrain, and the model has not yet been validated against yield records.

Use of AI. Built with AI assistance: the code, text and data in this project were generated with Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by the team.
